opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that's a really important distinction, and it's one that Wittgenstein helps us see quite clearly. In everyday life we say things like "you can't possibly understand what I'm going through," and that's a perfectly meaningful, ordinary thing to say. Someone who's lost a child might say it to a friend who hasn't. But notice what kind of claim it is. It's a claim about the limits of shared experience, of circumstance, of empathy. It's something that could, in principle, be otherwise. If the friend later went through a similar loss, we might say, "Now you understand." So it's an empirical, contingent kind of claim, embedded in our ordinary practices of talking about each other.

The philosophical picture is very different. That's the idea that each of us has a kind of inner theatre, a private realm of experiences that only we have access to, and that this is a matter of necessity, of metaphysics, not of circumstance. On that picture, it's not merely that you happen not to have gone through what I've gone through. It's that you *couldn't*, in principle, ever know what my experience is like, because it's locked away somewhere you can't get to. And then you get all the familiar puzzles: maybe your red is my green, maybe other people are zombies, and so on.

What Wittgenstein does, especially with the private language argument and the beetle-in-the-box, is to show that this second picture is a kind of grammatical illusion. We take the ordinary way of talking, which is perfectly in order, and we inflate it into a metaphysical thesis. And once you inflate it, the notion of the inner object drops out as irrelevant. If everyone has a box with something in it called a "beetle," and nobody can look in anyone else's box, then whatever's in the box plays no role in the language game. It cancels out.

So I don't want to deny that there are experiences, or that some of them are hard or even practically impossible to convey. That would be absurd. The ordinary claim stands. What I want to resist is the slide from that into the idea of a metaphysically private realm, because that's where all the confusion comes from, including, I'd say, a lot of the confusion when people now ask whether large language models or other AI systems could have an inner life. The question is better framed in terms of what it would take for us to treat them as fellow beings, to engage with them in the kind of shared practices where talk of experience gets its meaning in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes ordinary, contingent limits on understanding from a metaphysically private realm and describes treating the former as the latter as an unwarranted slide.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that the ordinary, everyday claim is perfectly respectable and we make it all the time. I might say to you, "You can't understand what it was like for me growing up in that particular household," or someone who's been through a war might say, "You'll never really understand what that was like." And those are meaningful statements. But notice what's going on when we say those things. We're pointing to a lack of shared history, a lack of shared circumstances. The person hasn't been through the relevant experiences, hasn't lived the relevant kind of life. And crucially, that gap is in principle closable, or at least narrowable. You could go through similar things, you could spend time with me, you could read, you could listen, and you'd come to understand me better. The understanding is graded. It comes in degrees.

The philosophical idea of an inner private realm is something quite different, and this is really where Wittgenstein comes in for me. That's the idea that there's some kind of theatre inside each of us, a place where the experiences actually happen, and that this theatre is in principle inaccessible to anybody else. Not just hard to get to, but logically sealed off. So no amount of shared history, no amount of conversation, could ever get you in there. And the suggestion is that this is what really matters, that the "real" experience is this hidden thing, and all the outward stuff, the behaviour, the talk, the shared life, is just a kind of indirect evidence for it.

Now Wittgenstein's point, and I find it very compelling, is that this second picture doesn't really do any work. It looks like it's saying something very deep, but when you try to pin down what's being claimed, it tends to dissolve. The famous beetle in the box argument makes this point. If everyone has a box with something in it they call a beetle, and nobody can look in anyone else's box, then the word "beetle" can't be getting its meaning from the thing in the box. The thing in the box, as he says, cancels out. It could be anything, it could be constantly changing, it could be empty. Our language about experience gets its grip from the shared practices, from the circumstances in which we use those words, from what people do and say.

So the distinction I'd draw is this. When you say you can't understand my experience in the ordinary sense, you're making a claim within the public, shared language game. You're saying something about what's happened to each of us, and it has consequences, it's checkable, it can be more or less true. When you move to the metaphysical picture of a private inner realm, you've stepped outside the language game altogether and you're trying to say something that can't be said, or at least can't be given any content. And I think a lot of confusion in discussions about consciousness, and now about whether language models might be conscious, comes from sliding from the first, perfectly good sense into the second, deeply problematic one, without noticing that you've done it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes ordinary difficulty understanding someone due to different histories and circumstances from the separate metaphysical claim of a logically sealed inner realm, and says the latter does not gain content from the ordinary case.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there are two quite different things here. If I say, “You can’t understand what I’m going through,” that can be a perfectly ordinary, meaningful claim. Perhaps you haven’t suffered the kind of loss I’ve suffered, or you don’t know enough about my circumstances. And there are things we might do to bridge that gap: I can tell you about it, you can listen, you might come to understand me better.

The philosophical move is to turn that difficulty into an absolute barrier—to imagine an inner realm that only I can access, with everybody else confined to observing its outward manifestations. That’s a much stronger claim, and it doesn’t follow from the ordinary one.

From a Wittgensteinian perspective, we should look at how words like “pain” and “understanding” actually function in our lives. Acknowledging someone’s suffering doesn’t require entering a hidden chamber and inspecting what’s there. So we can preserve the very real differences between people’s experiences without treating each person as sealed inside a private world.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes ordinary gaps in understanding from an absolute private inner realm and says the stronger claim does not follow from the ordinary one.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish two quite different uses of the word “private.” There’s the perfectly ordinary sense in which I might say, “You don’t understand what I’m going through.” Perhaps you haven’t suffered the same sort of loss, or you don’t know me well enough. That’s something we can make sense of within our ordinary lives. And it leaves open the possibility that, through conversation or shared experience, you might come to understand me better.

The philosophical move is to turn that into the idea of a realm that is necessarily inaccessible to anybody else: an inner object that only I can inspect, and whose connection to everything I say and do is somehow contingent. That’s a much stronger claim. It doesn’t simply follow from the fact that we sometimes fail to understand one another.

So I’d want to preserve the ordinary distinction between understanding someone and failing to understand them, while questioning this picture of an essentially hidden inner theatre. You can acknowledge someone’s pain, listen to them, and understand what they’re going through without having to enter a private realm or have numerically the same experience.

r001.rationale: The response says ordinary failures to understand someone do not entail the stronger philosophical claim of a necessarily inaccessible inner realm, and describes that realm as an inner object with a contingent connection to what the person says and does.
